lead: A communication system carries a message from a source to a destination through a channel that weakens the signal, adds noise and is shared with other users. Modulation moves the message spectrum up to a carrier frequency so that the signal suits the antenna, its licensed frequency slot and the channel. Every phone call, FM broadcast and UPI payment alert passes through the same chain of blocks.
prereq: You need: a sinusoid, frequency, wavelength and the relation c = fλ from first-year physics.

sections.h3: The block schematic of a communication system

blocks.text: A communication system moves information from a source to a destination. Information is whatever the destination does not already know: a voice, a temperature reading, a payment record, a frame of video. The system is drawn as a chain of blocks; some syllabi call this drawing the block schematic or the communication model.

The information source produces the message. An input transducer converts it into an electrical voltage: a microphone turns sound pressure into a voltage, a camera sensor turns light into charge. The result is the message signal m(t), a voltage that varies with time t in seconds. In Figure 1.1.1 the input transducer sits inside the source block, and the output transducer (a loudspeaker or a screen) sits inside the destination block.

The transmitter prepares the signal for the channel: it filters, modulates and amplifies. The channel is the physical medium: a copper pair, a coaxial cable, an optical fibre or free space. The receiver filters and amplifies what arrives, removes the carrier and produces an estimate m̂(t) of the message. The destination is a listener, a screen or a storage device.

blocks.where: r(t) is the received voltage; s(t) is the transmitted signal after the channel has attenuated it; n(t) is the unwanted noise voltage added by the channel and by the receiver's own circuits.

blocks.text: Noise is random, so it is described by statistics rather than by a formula; see Noise sources, white noise and AWGN. When m(t) is sent as a continuous waveform the system is analog. When the message is first turned into bits and the transmitter sends one of a finite set of waveforms, the system is digital; it adds a source encoder (compression) and a channel encoder (error protection) after the source, which are covered with information theory and coding.

sections.h3: Baseband, passband and modulation as frequency translation

blocks.text: A signal whose spectrum lies between 0 Hz and some highest frequency B hertz is a baseband signal. Speech, music and sensor outputs are baseband. A passband signal has its spectrum concentrated around a carrier frequency fc far above 0 Hz.

blocks.where: s(t) is the modulated (passband) signal; A(t) is its slowly varying envelope in volts; f<sub>c</sub> is the carrier frequency in hertz; φ(t) is its slowly varying phase in radians.

blocks.text: The carrier is the sinusoid cos(2πfct). It carries no information by itself; it only gives the signal a place in the spectrum. Modulation varies the carrier with m(t). If the amplitude A(t) follows m(t), the scheme is amplitude modulation (AM, with its forms DSB-SC, SSB and VSB). If the frequency or the phase φ(t) follows m(t), it is angle modulation: frequency modulation (FM) or phase modulation (PM). In digital modulation the same quantities are switched between a finite set of values.

Multiplying m(t) by cos(2πfct) copies the message spectrum to −fc and +fc; Fourier transform review and band-pass signals proves this. Modulation creates no new information; it moves the information to a new place in the spectrum. The width Bs of the band the modulated signal occupies is its bandwidth; for AM, Bs = 2B. The bandwidth is set by the message and the scheme, not by fc.

items: Antenna size. An antenna radiates well when its length is a good fraction of the wavelength λ = c/f, where c = 3×108 m/s and f is the radiated frequency in hertz. A quarter-wave antenna is λ/4 long: kilometres at audio frequencies, centimetres to metres at radio frequencies. The worked example computes both.

Frequency assignment. Free space is shared by everyone. Regulators license bands (mobile services in India use bands near 900 MHz, 1800 MHz and 3.5 GHz) so that each transmitter stays inside its own slot. Modulation puts a signal into its assigned slot.

Multiplexing. Many messages share one channel when each sits on a different carrier: frequency division multiplexing (FDM). Time division multiplexing shares the time axis instead and is covered with pulse modulation.

Noise and interference. Modulation does not remove noise. It moves the signal to a band where interference is low, and the receiver's band-pass filter keeps only fc − Bs/2 to fc + Bs/2. Wideband FM goes further and trades extra bandwidth for a better output signal-to-noise ratio.

Propagation. Each frequency range travels differently: medium-wave broadcasts near 1 MHz follow the ground for long distances, while VHF and higher bands travel in near line of sight. The carrier is chosen to suit the distance to be covered.

examples.question: A 1 kHz audio tone has to be radiated from an antenna. (a) Find its wavelength and the length of a quarter-wave antenna. (b) The same tone now modulates a 100 MHz carrier. Find the wavelength and the quarter-wave antenna length of the radiated wave. Take c = 3×10<sup>8</sup> m/s.
steps: Use λ = c/f. At f = 1 kHz = 1×10<sup>3</sup> Hz: λ = (3×10<sup>8</sup> m/s) ÷ (1×10<sup>3</sup> Hz) = 3×10<sup>5</sup> m = 300 km.
Quarter-wave length = λ/4 = 300 km ÷ 4 = 75 km. No tower can hold a 75 km antenna, so the audio tone cannot be radiated directly.
At the carrier f<sub>c</sub> = 100 MHz = 1×10<sup>8</sup> Hz: λ = (3×10<sup>8</sup> m/s) ÷ (1×10<sup>8</sup> Hz) = 3 m.
Quarter-wave length = λ/4 = 3 m ÷ 4 = 0.75 m, that is 75 cm: a small, practical antenna.

Check: the antenna shrank by 75 km ÷ 0.75 m = 1×10<sup>5</sup>, which is exactly the ratio of the two frequencies, 100 MHz ÷ 1 kHz. The audio still reaches the listener, carried as a variation of the envelope A(t) or the phase φ(t).
examples.answer: At 1 kHz: λ = 300 km and λ/4 = 75 km. At 100 MHz: λ = 3 m and λ/4 = 0.75 m. Modulation shortens the antenna by a factor of 10<sup>5</sup>.

traps: Modulation does not create information and does not by itself improve the signal-to-noise ratio at the receiver input. It shifts the message spectrum so that the antenna, the frequency plan and multiplexing become practical.
Do not confuse the carrier frequency with the message frequency. The carrier decides where the signal sits in the spectrum; the message and the scheme decide the bandwidth.
In λ = c/f, put the frequency that is actually radiated. After modulation that is f<sub>c</sub>, not the audio frequency.
The receiver filter is centred on f<sub>c</sub> and is B<sub>s</sub> wide in total, from f<sub>c</sub> − B<sub>s</sub>/2 to f<sub>c</sub> + B<sub>s</sub>/2, not f<sub>c</sub> ± B<sub>s</sub>.
Baseband does not mean audio. Any signal whose spectrum starts at 0 Hz, including a train of digital pulses, is a baseband signal.

quiz.q: List the blocks of a communication system in order from source to destination.
quiz.a: Information source (with its input transducer), transmitter, channel, receiver, destination (with its output transducer). Noise n(t) adds to the signal in the channel and in the receiver front end.

The carrier is the high-frequency sinusoid cos(2πf<sub>c</sub>t) that places the signal in the spectrum. The message signal m(t) is the baseband voltage from the source and its transducer; it carries the information.

quiz.q: Why must a baseband audio signal be modulated before free-space transmission?
quiz.a: At audio frequencies the wavelength is hundreds of kilometres, so a quarter-wave antenna would be tens of kilometres long. Modulation moves the spectrum to a radio frequency where λ/4 is under a metre, places the signal in its licensed slot, and lets the receiver filter out other users.

quiz.q: Modulation does not improve the signal-to-noise ratio at the receiver input. State three things it does achieve.
quiz.a: It makes the antenna small enough to build; it places each signal in an assigned frequency slot so many users share the medium by FDM; it lets the receiver band-pass filter away interference outside its own band.

quiz.q: A 4 kHz message is sent by AM on a 10 MHz carrier. Find the carrier wavelength, the quarter-wave antenna length and the bandwidth of the modulated signal.
quiz.a: λ = c/f<sub>c</sub> = (3×10<sup>8</sup>) ÷ (1×10<sup>7</sup>) = 30 m. λ/4 = 7.5 m. B<sub>s</sub> = 2B = 8 kHz, from 9.996 MHz to 10.004 MHz.

quiz.q: Two stations in one city each carry a 5 kHz audio message by AM. Explain why they cannot both use a 1 MHz carrier, and find the smallest carrier spacing.
quiz.a: Each AM signal occupies 2B = 10 kHz, from 0.995 MHz to 1.005 MHz. On the same carrier the two spectra lie on top of each other, so no filter can separate them. Each signal reaches 5 kHz on either side of its carrier, so the carriers must be at least 5 + 5 = 10 kHz apart (in practice more, to leave a guard band).

quiz.q: One system sends a 5 kHz message over a cable at baseband; another sends it by AM on a 1 GHz carrier over free space. Compare their bandwidths and antenna needs.
quiz.a: The cable system occupies 0 to 5 kHz, so B = 5 kHz. The AM system occupies 2B = 10 kHz around 1 GHz: twice as wide, set by the scheme and not by the carrier. The cable needs no antenna. The radio link needs one of about λ/4 = 0.3 m ÷ 4 = 7.5 cm at 1 GHz; without the carrier, a 5 kHz antenna would be λ/4 = 60 km ÷ 4 = 15 km.

beyond: Not for the exam. A software-defined radio samples the passband or downconverted signal and does the mixing, filtering and demodulation in code, so one piece of hardware serves many standards. In 5G and Wi-Fi the carrier sits in the gigahertz range, which is why a handset holds several small antennas and why millimetre-wave links need line of sight. Spectrum is auctioned as a national resource, and the price of a band is the price of a place for the carrier. Search for software-defined radio, spectrum auction and link budget to go further.
